utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down. Good morning again, sir. May I remind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish good morning to everyone and may there be peace in this house and may God's will be done in this proceedings as well, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. And I would also like to ask the witness to just pause after my question before answering, and I will do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, I asked you about some things that you were also asked by the Prosecutor, and on page 64 of yesterday's transcript, line 20, the following was said: You would issue an order to the military police to bring in so and so. Now I would like to ask you this: Were you -- did you have the right to issue orders to the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that right. However, when -- where it concerned men from my battalion, I would send an order in writing that those men should be taken over or brought over; that was the rule. We would use the radio and we would say, "Such and such should do this or that," and that would then be relayed to the military police, and then they would bring in those people according or pursuant to my orders, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you, according to the battalion plan, issue orders to the military police of the superior unit?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us for the transcript what the difference is between an order and instructions, "Nalog" and "Naredjenje" in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a big difference. The military police belonged to the brigade and all I did was send instructions, nalog, for certain men to be taken into custody or to be brought in. If they didn't, I could not issue an order. I could only appeal or I could only complain to the brigade chief if an instructions that I issued were not followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your platoon commanders and company commanders first inform you who was missing and then, based on that, you would issue your instructions to the competent authorities or competent superior who could issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When the issue is absence without leave, absence from combat, because that's what we are talking about here, would the command then pay special attention to such matters and I'm referring here to the brigade commander all the way down to the platoon commander. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a procedure to be followed, and it went the same way. On orders from the battalion commanders, that person, who is absent, would be reported to the brigade command, it would be reported that the person was absent without leave. However, this was done through the battalion commander and the brigade commander. In other words, what to do with such men who would just go without leave from the battalion or from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's not discuss specific issues so it is sufficient just for these purposes to say that there was -- it was necessary to have the instructions of the brigade -- of the battalion commander, is that how it always transpired, it always had to go through the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was always done and we were all of us were subordinate to the battalion commander. He was the only person who could actually punish a soldier by -- with a punishment of a seven-day imprisonment and that was the only person that could mete out such punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It appears there may be some confusion in the record because the previous answer on page 3, line 7 and 8, referred to the brigade commander, and the authority of the brigade commander. Then the following question related to the brigade commander as well and then the answer responded to the battalion commander. So I just wanted to be sure that we are all talking about the same thing or what it is we are talking about, in terms of the subordination as the witness has just mentioned to the battalion commander or to the brigade commander. So I'd appreciate it if General Tolimir could clarify that with the witness so that the record is clear before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, on line 7 and 8 of page 3, the witness is recorded to having said: "However, this was done through the battalion commander and the brigade commander." He was referring to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, you'll see Mr. President, page 3, line 16, the witness says: "Yes, that's how it was always done and we were all of us subordinate to the battalion commander," which wouldn't include the brigade commander and the power to punish resided essentially in the brigade commander, and that's something that I think that needs to be clarified with the witness for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you please clarify this problem with the witness with your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I would like to thank Mr. Vanderpuye. I cannot really follow the transcript so I will again ask the witness to tell us whether all the activities that were going in the direction to the brigade, the security organ from the battalion had to carry them out with the approval of the brigade command -- battalion commander, no matter what issues were concerned.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, here let's go again to page 62 of the transcript, line 2. Mr. Vanderpuye asked you whether yesterday it was your duty first to inform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt you because I don't know if you misspoke first or it was a problem of the interpretation. Now we see that: "The security organ from the battalion had to carry them out with the approval of the brigade command -- battalion commander no matter what issues were concerned." These words of yours were recorded. That didn't help to bring some clarity in the matter. Could you please repeat in more detail what was the chain of communication in this respect, sir? This is now a question for you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the battalion, and I'm talking about what the Prosecutor was asking me, was what to do with the men who were absent without leave under normal circumstances. I explained then that we would send instructions to the military police, sometimes we would use the radio, to bring in those men because the military police was the only one which had the right to go and search for the person, whether that person was at home or some place else. But the battalion commander would have to be informed of all that. As for the second part, that is not clear perhaps is that in the event that somebody deserted from the battalion or just fled during combat, that then would be an infraction that was of higher severity and, and in that case the battalion commander would inform the brigade commander of such instances, and that would then no longer be within the competence of the battalion or the security organ within the battalion, but rather the battalion commander would inform thereof the brigade commander and then they would resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope everybody has now a clear picture. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, tell us, please, as the security organ within the battalion, did you ever have the right to have direct contacts, official contacts, with the brigade commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. However, I could resort to that in the event -- well, let me just give you an example. If it was necessary to complain about poor work being done by the battalion commander or his deputy, then I could directly inform the brigade -- the security officer, but -- of the brigade but I could also inform the brigade commander but only in the instances that had to do with poor work or incompetence within the battalion. In other words, if the battalion was put in jeopardy, if the front line was weakened through such incompetence. So I could only inform the chief of security or the brigade chief in those instances where there was a problem with battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the same right that -- where every superior -- every officer has the right to report his superior officer for the poor work of his superior, direct superior?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, yesterday you were asked by the Prosecutor whether it was your duty to inform your commander, the military police, or your security organ, which was -- which had the priority? And whether the military police then had to take action pursuant to your complaints or your reports. In answer to the second question, you've already said what it was but I will give you an opportunity to answer that question again. But let me ask you this: Did you first inform your battalion commander and only then go outside of your battalion to report that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was standard practice for men to frequently be absent from the battalion or to come to the front line late, and we, of course, never knew -- when I say we, I mean the men in the battalion, we never knew when we would be attacked, so it was our duty to make sure that the front line always had a sufficient number of men according to previous plans, and according to how it was determined in advance. Now, when some personnel were absent I would inform the battalion commander thereof, but if the battalion commander wasn't there, then I could issue instructions to the military police to bring in those men. I could not issue an order to them but, based on those instructions, I could only send, usually by radio, instructions and I would have to sign it so that they would know who it was sent from, but in my absence it could be done by the battalion commander or even his deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to make sure that we are talking about the context of the witness's capacity as an assistant commander for security and intelligence in the battalion as distinguished from his capacity as the deputy battalion commander, in the context of this question, because it wasn't framed in the question that was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, as you know from yesterday that the witness changed his post in March 1995. It is important to know if your questions are referring to the period after March 1995 or before March 1995. Please clarify that with the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 62, line 2, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you if it was your duty, if it had been your duty to first report to your commander in other words, that was during the period of time when he had a commander. He said or the military police or your security chief. So having read the question that had been put to him then, I understood the question to mean that he had a commander at the time, he wasn't acting independently. But let's clarify since the witness is being treated here as an individual who had power to do something, tell us, Witness, how do you distinguish between an instruction and a warrant for arrest? Because if there is a warrant for arrest, there is no instruction, is there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I would write an instruction in the battalion, I couldn't take it to the brigade HQ which was some ten kilometres away, and then we would have several instructions a day, so we would transmit these instructions by radio and then these instructions would be in written form taken to the military police who would be informed that such and such a senior officer from the battalion issued these instructions for those people to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's clarify this. What you transmitted by radio, was that an instruction or was it a request for those people to be brought in because there is a clear difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably a request. I don't know how we called it but it was, I think more likely to have been a request than an instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, was that -- the last answer, Witness, were you referring to the period after March 1995 or before March 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of this referred to the period up to March of 1995, when I was assistant commander for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, just a moment. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, witness. I have a question for clarification purposes. Before March 1995, you were assistant battalion -- assistant commander for security and intelligence at battalion level but within the Zvornik Brigade, is that it? Could you tell me what were the specific duties of the assistant commander for security and intelligence at battalion level in relation to the functions of the company of a -- of the company -- of the military police company brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said earlier on, my duty was to monitor certain activities within the battalion and report anything that I felt was necessary to be reported to the battalion commander. Now, as for the military police company commander, his duty was to accommodate the requests that we sent to him concerning our soldiers that needed taking into custody. Other than that we didn't have any obligations in either way. The duty of the military police was to locate these people, to take them into custody, and that was what they needed to do on their part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you see, this seemingly insignificant question is very important, both to Their Honours and the OTP and us. We also need to hear from you what duties of a security organ were. I'll give you an opportunity to do that. Now, you referred to an obligation. Did the military police have an obligation towards you, or not? Because these are different matters. If he considers your request, for instance, to take soldiers into custody an obligation on his part or whether he could prioritise his tasks as this was only one among the duties he had to attend to.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was performing my duties, I wasn't trained sufficiently to know exactly which of the roles carried which of these duties. I think that the police had the obligation to meet these requests, but was also able to not do it. The only thing we could have done, absent his follow-up, was to report that particular military policeman to his superiors in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be very precise when referring to these various orders. Are these instructions that you issued him or whatever they are, is it something that he would be held accountable for to you or to his superior officers?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answers are probably down to the fact that I am not versed enough in these issues of orders, because I -- and requests, because I simply didn't attend any military schools. I think I performed to the best of my abilities at the time, but don't expect me to be able to distinguish between requests and instructions and orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please don't apologise to me; you're simply a witness here. You say he had to carry out that task. Did he have to fulfil this as a task or was it a request?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that he had his duties within the brigade. Now, it was down to some other individuals who would assess what had to be done and what didn't have to be done. If we failed to do something, we would have been discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm merely asking you to use the terminology in no uncertain terms. You said that you would give tasks to the brigade military police. Were they really tasks, these that you were issuing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes the witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped the witness because it's very difficult again for the interpreters to catch what you are saying. You are overlapping. You have to pause between question and answer and question again. It was very difficult. Mr. Vanderpuye and then the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see that we are bogged down, as it were, in terms of specific military definitions or definitions that General Tolimir wishes to use with the witness. The witness has indicated on a number of occasions he's not specifically versed in these kinds of qualifications, different definitions. It might be helpful if General Tolimir put to the witness what General Tolimir's understanding is of what an order is, a task is, an instruction is, so that the witness can better understand what it is General Tolimir's question concerns and can better explain what his specific activities were in relation to those functions as an assistant commander for security at the battalion level. It's just a suggestion. It's not an objection. But I think it will make things go a little bit more smoothly than they have been so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this proposal is very helpful because Mr. Tolimir is not giving evidence but the witness is giving evidence and we want to know what he knows about these matters, and therefore I think the witness should answer the last -- try to answer the last question, and Mr. Tolimir said, "You said that you would give tasks to the brigade military police. Were they really task, these that you were issuing?" I think it is a quite simple question and the witness is in the position to try to answer this. Thank you. I repeated the question of Mr. Tolimir. You already started your answer but I interrupted you because of the overlapping speaking. Would you please provide us with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We in the battalion could not issue orders to the military police or their commander to carry out our tasks. What we could do was to send requests from the battalion which had to do directly with battalion members, and then on the basis of these requests they would take the soldiers concerned into custody. So from the battalion level to the brigade level, and that's what they could do. They were entitled to do so because they had the military police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. We will also accommodate what the OTP needs. At the time when you were charged with security affairs within the battalion, did you put in place procedures and measures issued by your battalion command with a view to implementing security-related measures as dictated by superior commands?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now have D148 shown to the witness? D148. Page 66 in Serbian and 38 in English. Thank you. You see item 122, we have it in English as well which reads: "The security organ is a specialised organ of the command which organises and implements measures and procedures of counterintelligence support. It also participates in recommending, organising and implementing security and self-protection measures which concern," and I emphasise this, "The command and other subjects of self protection." So is it -- is this the basis from which your obligations toward your command stemmed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But whether I am -- I was a specialist organ or not is a different matter. For the rest, these were our obligations within the battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in addition to you, at a time when you were assistant commander for security, was there anyone else who had higher expertise and authority to deal with these matters?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nobody else except me within the battalion charged with security and intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at page 65 in Serbian and 38 in English. Yesterday, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you if you had also carried out -- if you had carried out the activities concerning both security and intelligence, and your answer was in the affirmative. I will first read out the relevant portion and then put the question. You can see there it says, "The intelligence organ. The intelligence organ is responsible for and organises intelligence support for combat actions, it continuously monitors and assesses the enemy and reports the enemy's condition to everybody concerned in the command. It suggests to the commander or Chief of Staff the procedure and resources for intelligence support for the brigade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, that was paragraph 118.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, this is my question: Did you give proposals to the commander or Chief of Staff for measures and activities, or did you have the right to also issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the right to issue orders. I had the right to give my proposals to the commander. Any subsequent activities related to the enemy, its advancement or regrouping, lay solely within the competence of the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. In order not to have some matters left unclarified, please answer this question: At a later date, as deputy commander and at an even later date as an acting commander, did you have the right to issue orders to anyone from a different organic unit and your superior unit, i.e. the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the right to issue orders to anyone. I was solely tied to my battalion. Any unit which would be seconded to assist my battalion, either at the level of a platoon or be it two platoons, would be within my competence if within my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 68, line 12 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you if you, as assistant commander for intelligence and security, had had the authority to report any crime committed within your battalion. This is my question, if you recall this: Were you able to make decisions independently as to what sort of an attitude you would take toward a perpetrator of a crime within your battalion at a time when you were assistant commander for security and intelligence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I already explained this. They were within the exclusive jurisdiction of the battalion commander, not his deputy, and not his assistant for security. He could only issue measure up to 7 days of military detention for the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So now that we are talking about filing complaints, I want to ask you, would you normally file a complaint about any negative activity that you noticed within the battalion while you were at the position of the acting commander and the deputy commander? I assume that the Prosecutor asked you about this period. So my question is: Would you get in touch with the brigade command when you would find that there were certain negative activities at the location where you would send your soldiers pursuant to the request of your superior?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained everything. Are you talking about the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from a soldier who was up on the line. I went to the duty officer in the battalion to ask what was going on, they wouldn't tell me anything. Later on, I managed to learn more through a certain person, and when Mr. Trbic called me, I did what I did because the only person at that moment who could order me something or who could give me some instructions was at the moment Major Obrenovic, and I couldn't get in touch with him because he was in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again I think we have some issues with respect to the interpretation. Here, at page 16, line 18, I have it in the transcript, 17 and 18, the witness says, "I went to the duty officer in the battalion to ask what was going on." I think it's clear from the record, from the transcript, that, in fact, he went to the duty -- he inquired with the duty office of the brigade, not the battalion. I don't know whether or not that's what he said or misspoke but this is I think a rather important issue because in relation to his duties and functions it is important this to have a very clear record on whether he's talking about the battalion or the superior command in the brigade, and that's what I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, can you help us? You are recorded to having said, "I heard that from a soldier who was up on the line. I went to the duty officer in the battalion to ask what was going on. They wouldn't tell me anything." Now, are you saying battalion or brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go there. I just called the duty officer in the brigade by phone. I couldn't go there. So I called them. I called the duty officer in the brigade and I wanted him to tell me what was going on in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That clarifies the situation. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ristic, the Prosecutor just emphasised how important this is. So I would like you to be very precise and specific in your answers. Don't say anything that could be understood in more than one way. I'm going to repeat the question. You probably know why he asked you. Did you report, did you file any complaint about any negative things that you saw going on in the village, in which your soldiers took part as tasked by the superior command? So I want a very short answer. Did you report that to the brigade command and that would be the duty officer in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I answered -- and I received the answer, Just go on, do your job, this is nothing to do with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you later on, on your own initiative, withdraw your soldiers because these tasks were inappropriate for soldiers to carry out?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you held responsible later on because you did something on your own initiative and withdrew your soldiers preventing them thereby to carry out the task that they had been assigned earlier?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not held responsible. Nobody asked me ever anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 1D556, 1D556? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tolimir, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a question from the witness. Can you tell me when you were acting commander and for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was acting commander from the 1st of July until the 18th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, here on the screen in front of you, you can see the statement that you gave on the 18th of October 2005. The subject matter of this statement is the same as the subject matter of your present testimony. I would like to have now page 41 in Serbian and 31 in English. So this is your interrogation by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal in 2005. Thank you. This has to do with your relations with your superiors. The investigator asked you, that's the 10th line on the page, line 20 in English, "Did you ever talk to Pandurevic about what happened at Orahovac?" And you said no. "Did you ever talk to Trbic about it?" You say, "Although I wanted to talk about it, none of them wanted to discuss it or to analyse it." "But did you ever ask Drago Nikolic about it?" "Yes, I did." "What did you say to Drago?" And then you say, "I asked him what happened in Orahovac. And I asked him about the prisoners. He told me that he was also caught by that because he also believed that they would be taken to Batkovici and he thought that they would be put up there just temporarily, and that's why he allegedly picked the school in Orahovac which was close to the line because he thought they would not stay there very long. That's what he said." So based on this, my question is as follows: Based on everything that you saw, are you convinced that Nikolic really told you that and that the Zvornik Brigade and your superiors were really surprised by the fact that the prisoners were deployed inside their zone?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Drago Nikolic said that to me. As far as other members of the Zvornik Brigade are concerned, I don't know whether they were taken by surprise or not, but I asked Drago Nikolic because, from 1992 to 1995, Muslim soldiers and civilians used to cross the area of Crni Vrh and that part of Baljkovica moving towards Nezuk. We used to have double guards there because we never knew when they were going to pass. Bearing in mind that Orahovac is in a valley, and there is a Muslim village, Krizevici, up towards Crni Vrh, a deserted Muslim village, and since there was a possibility that those who passed over Crni Vrh could see those assembled around the school is, so all this in my opinion could have caused an attack on this village by the soldiers from Srebrenica. So I spoke to Drago about this issue, why they came to Orahovac, and when I asked him that, that's what he answered me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer was a bit longer than unusual, so the essence of your answer to my question was actually lost. I'm now going to repeat my question and I want you to answer succinctly. Was Drago Nikolic surprised by the fact that the Muslim prisoners were brought to the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what he told me, yes, he was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you surprised by the deployment of Muslim prisoners into the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Your soldiers on the line, were they surprised and did they protest about it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were surprised and they didn't like the fact that the prisoners were brought to Orahovac, and generally in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering that Drago thought that they would be exchanged and that he put them close to the line because exchanges are performed across lines, can you tell us, is there a possibility that somebody after they had been brought into your zone changed the decision about their exchange? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was some change in the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see the question has been answered but I would ask General Tolimir to refrain from asking completely speculative questions. It doesn't seem that this is something that is in the know of this witness, that's within his ken, to ask whether there is the possibility that somebody might have changed plans really doesn't advance any -- any probative interest in the case. The answer is that there's always a possibility. There is a possibility of many, many different things and so I think, despite the fact that the witness has answered the question, I have made the objection just so the Trial Chamber is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The question is answered, indeed. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. This witness commanded the battalion during a period of 18 days, and he knew; he did not assume things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that your soldiers were protesting because of the deployment of Muslims within Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's how I found out that they came, because it was a man from this particular village who protested. He was up at the defence line as a member of the 2nd Company. His family lives in Orahovac close to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you personally protest by means of telephone calls to the brigade command when you found out about it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I protested. If at the time I had the possibility to get in touch with the Chief of Staff or the brigade commander, then I probably would have protested about the fact that somebody brought them into this area. And I explained why I would have made such a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Drago Nikolic tell you that he was surprised by the fact that they were brought there and that he expected them to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what I said in my statement, that is exactly what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are these your assumptions or is this based on actual facts and events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are actual facts. We spoke about it, and I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you, as the commander of the battalion, were you also able to see, based on some other events that took place at the same time and based on what you learned as acting commander, is it possible that somebody changed the decision about those prisoners, the decision that they should be exchanged, after they arrived into your zone?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my conversation with Drago Nikolic, there was probably some sort of change, if all this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Tolimir? On page 22, lines 8 through 11, I need a clarification. Sir, you were asked by Mr. Tolimir if you protested, and your answer was: "I protested. If at that time I had the possibility to get in touch with the Chief of Staff of the -- or the brigade commander, then I probably would have protested about the fact." Did you protest or would you have liked to protest but you didn't? I don't understand that. What really, in fact, did you do at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the duty officer what was going on. Now, exactly what kind of answer I received from him and whether exactly it was the duty officer or somebody else, I was not able to judge. I already said that I asked to speak to the chief of the brigade because I wanted to ask him what was going on. I received the same response. I was told that he was in the zone of Kamenica and Snagovo. So in this moment, I simply didn't have a way to protest or to complain to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can take it that the first part of your previous answer, "I protested," was not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can be interpreted as me not protesting because I didn't know what was going on. I first asked the duty officer at the operations room what was going on because I didn't know what was being done. I didn't even know that they had come, until I was told by the person I called, in order to ask them about what was going on in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the brigade at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vinko Pandurevic was at the head of the brigade, and the chief was Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you, Witness. My apologies for bringing you in -- putting you in this spot, as it were, by my question -- by putting these questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask you, the battalion commander, when you -- when you called the duty officer, did you, as a battalion commander, have any other option other than to call the operations office and the duty officer at the brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was standard practice that any queries that we had, that had to do with the brigade, we would have to put through the duty officer. In spite of the fact that I was battalion commander it was not standard practice for me to get in touch directly with the brigade commander or the chief. We would always submit our requests or queries through the duty officer and that's how we would request to get in touch with them, either by phone or in person where they would come to see us or we would go and see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether this practice of the subordinates to communicate with their superiors via the duty officer, was that the practice that was put in place by the brigade command or by the subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was put in place by the brigade command. We were told that that's what we should do and that's how we always did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether this was done to prevent people from calling all the time and actually interfering with the work of the commander, that that's why they would have to go through the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because of that, because the brigade command and the chief of the command, they had other responsibilities that had to do with other battalions, with the corps, other brigades, so that we couldn't just interrupt them all the time, and a lot of information was relayed to us through the duty officer and if there was an urgent matter that needed to be resolved, we would ask the duty officer as to whether we could contact, get in touch with either the brigade commander or the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when at their request you sent ten of your soldiers in order to stand guard at the school, did you do this because it was necessary because you wanted to actually appease the concern that the people from the village had?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After this, did the protests and the revolt that you could see from the conscripts who were within your battalion and who wanted to go home, did it end after you've done this?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview that we saw before us, did you explain to the investigators and the Prosecutors about the channel through which you had to communicate with your superiors and how you put questions about what was going on in Orahovac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which superiors are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll be specific. Did the investigator ask you whether you had ever discussed the circumstances and the events at the Orahovac school with Obrenovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all of this ended, and after I was demobilised, Obrenovic came to the village to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My apologies. Could you please just answer my question with a "yes" or "no", and then tell us what you did?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, we'll miss your answer.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did discuss this with him. Do you want me now to explain what it was that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you about that but if you feel that you want to, you can tell us. So you did have occasion to see him.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor, let me just say that this conversation that you had with Obrenovic was something that was mentioned on pages 27 and 28 of your statement, 1D557, where we can see that you didn't try to conceal anything and that you said as much to -- during this interview with the investigators. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could I just see it before me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up 1D557 in e-court for the benefit of the witness? That's page 28. Here we have the statement. We see it on the right-hand side. And that will be page 21 in English, and I thank Aleksandar for this. Paragraph 1. In English, that's the last paragraph and in Serbian that's the first paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that there is -- that there are only seven pages in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I may have misspoken. I should have asked for 1D556 and I said 1D557. Thank you, and my apologies to e-court. Could we now please pull up page 28 in Serbian? That's fine. It isn't? No, we don't see that exchange here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you could read on the page, and that's in the first paragraph in Serbian and the last paragraph in English, where we can see that you did talk about this issue, both with the Prosecutor and with your superiors. Now, if you've read the paragraph, can I put the question to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of this interview with the investigator, were you asked by the Prosecutor about these events and did he ask you about your conversation with Obrenovic about them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tell the Prosecutor that you actually had talked with Obrenovic about these events? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This conversation was about something else, but I asked him about the development -- the events in Baljkovica during combat and in Orahovac and he told me on that occasion that he hadn't known anything about what was going on in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to another statement of yours about these events during the period when you were acting commander, and if you have something to add, would you please do so now, because I frequently interrupted you and actually abbreviated your answers, as it were.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's all I had to say. You can go on with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please pull in e-court the document that I requested a little earlier, 1D557?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to put a question to the witness to clarify one answer. On page 23 -- 20, line 23, you were asked by Mr. Tolimir -- no, sorry, by Mr. Vanderpuye, "Your soldiers on the line, were they surprised and did they protest about it?" -- no, it's during cross-examination, of course, by Mr. Tolimir. Please switch off your microphone for a moment. And you were asked by Mr. Tolimir: "Your soldiers on the line, were they surprised, did they protest about it." And you said, "They were surprised and they didn't like the fact that the prisoners were brought to Orahovac." What happened with these soldiers? What did they do? Were they discussing with you or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were on the front line and I was at the battalion command. They asked me what was going on in Orahovac and why won't you tell us? I told them that I didn't know anything about it, that I would check and let them know. They told me then, "Let us know because we want to leave the front line. We want to go to our village to defend our children and our wives." This posed a big problem for me because they were in the central part of the area of responsibility of my battalion, deployed in several trenches at a critical point where there was a small river, a stream, rather, and I realised, because I didn't know anything about any Muslim deployments in front or on the other side of our area of responsibility, I knew that I would have a major problem if they were to leave the front line and I had no way of stopping them because the terrain around Baljkovica is very remote and very difficult to negotiate, so that later on I sought answers from others, I asked about this, and I asked others about what was going on down there so that they actually remained on the front line, they did not desert it. Now, what kind of conversation they may have had amongst them, I don't know, because I wasn't there but they were probably protesting and they were probably criticising everything because they were afraid for their own families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Would you call that a revolt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had I been there on the spot, I probably would have known, judging by what they were saying, whether this was a revolt or not, but there was a threat that they relayed to the battalion that they would do this unless they were given true information. Well, I don't know how better to describe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Tolimir. Now the document you requested is on the screen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You have actually made our job easier because we were -- I was going to request that document, page 3 of the document, paragraph 3, where the witness is describing exactly what he's just told us now and this was documented on the day when he provided his statement to the competent authorities about the developments and the revolt of his soldiers because of prisoners of war having been brought to their village. That's on page 4 in English, lines 1 through 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 14 you say the following and I quote: "I reported to 2nd Infantry Company that I would keep them informed and that they shouldn't leave the front line. And that I had sent men to help with defending -- with the defence of the village. Half of the men of the Intervention Platoon had remained in order to provide support to the sector of the Baljkovac area." Now my question is this: Are these your words? Did you say this while you were giving your statement in 2003 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What you say here, is that consistent with the events in that sector when you sent a portion of the Intervention Platoon at the request of Trbic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In combat, would any request from a combatant providing defences on the line, would you have to respond to that in order for them not to leave the line, the front line?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you had to do that or not, but however -- it was required, it was incumbent upon us to do that. We had to help the people who were deployed on the front lines. That's what we were there for. And I felt that it was my duty to help these men, whatever the situation may be, because they were in the forward lines of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to dwell on this issue any longer because you provided an extensive answer. Can we move to page 4 of this statement of yours in e-court? Paragraph 1. Line 2 through 10. Thank you. We can see it on our screens. I will read the beginning of the sentence so you know where we are and I'm quoting: "At around 1330 hours, Major Obrenovic came to the battalion command." That's page 6 in English. "Major Obrenovic arrived, as did Captain Milano Jolovic. A Praga arrived with a crew," et cetera. The last two lines read, "The attack lasted all day and until the following day, 1200 hours, when we left the command post and withdrew towards Parlog." Is what you are describing here related to the 15th and 16th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you suffer from this attack from both the front line and the rear on this day that you are describing here?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was it who attacked you from the front line?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intervention units of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did their attack ensue on this particular day, if you know, and what was the objective of the attack?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most probable objective was to secure a corridor for the passage of the Muslims from Srebrenica in the direction of Nezluk. Later on, we saw that the intended corridor had been marked out. The point of the attack was to remove us from the area, from the dugouts there, in order for them to have safe passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the purpose of the attack was to make their way through. Now, who was it who attacked and was their purpose to take up positions there, to capture the area? Please be precise.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was for them to take control of our trenches, to disperse our soldiers or to defeat them, from the 1st and parts of the 2nd Company because that was where they had designated the prospective corridor that was to be opened for the passage of the Muslims from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the term "passage." Did the Muslims pass through your area of responsibility or were they fighting their way through in order to seize the trenches that were the first line of our defence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were fighting their way to where our command was with a view to destroying our command post and going beyond or crossing our defence line. They had the support of the intervention units of the BH Army from the 2nd Corps, from the other end of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was there also a breach of your lines from the rear, from the direction of Srebrenica toward Nezluk?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a breach of our line because we had some 20 wounded soldiers, a couple of fatalities. They set our command post on fire. When we retreated and we were compelled to retreat at 12 -- around 1200 hours of the 16th, they advanced toward the command post, they set fire to the Praga, the command post and the buildings that we used as our living quarters. Thereupon our commander, in agreement with a commander who was stationed at Nezuk, reached a cease-fire agreement enabling the group of Muslims to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say here that there was an attack, that the command post and the Praga were set alight and so on and so forth. But did they have any casualties in this attempt to break through your forces and link up with the Muslim units beyond your front -- your positions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do suppose that they suffered some casualties as well because this was difficult terrain, mountainous, shells were landing, there was gunfire. I don't know how many casualties they had, either wounded or dead, because they took them along. They took whatever vehicles they could pick up along the way, in order to transport them further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since they transported these combat vehicles including casualties, did they also take along any of the soldiers that they may have taken prisoner from the command post that they had set on fire?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they had passed through, when our soldiers were gathering the dead, I saw the dead bodies lined up in a meadow before they were loaded on to TAMs. I was asked whether there were any of my men from my battalion, what I was able to see were dead bodies only without the presence of any weapons so I don't know what became of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you said when "our" men were gathering the dead, who precisely was gathering them and the dead, they were members of which units?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain that the TAM was the property of the unit of the Drina Wolves, in other words what I wanted to say was that the person calling to me didn't know who the dead bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat his question because they are overlapping? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you, I'm very sorry, the question was not very well recorded and interpreted because of overlapping again. Repeat the question, please. Then the answer. And then we must have our first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was collecting dead bodies in the area of responsibility of your battalion? Was it the Muslim or the Serb side? And where were the dead bodies taken to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Muslims passed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which passage are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I meant was that the Muslims had passed through and we were mopping up the area stretching between the location of our command post and the front lines. So there was a unit of the Drina Wolves which happened there because they had had their men fighting over there and they were gathering along the way all the dead bodies that they could find, and ultimately they placed them in a meadow before loading them on to a TAM. At that point they asked me if any of the dead used to belong to my battalion because they didn't know them. What they did next was that they transported these bodies by the TAM to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir. Sorry, nothing could be heard by the interpreters, the interpretation didn't stop yet. You started immediately again with your next question. Nobody can hear that. And I indicated earlier we must have the first break now. You should consider your next -- the course of your cross-examination and, please, no overlapping. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please be aware of the need to be very slow and to pause between question and answer. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I apologise to the interpreters once more for the difficulties we had in the latter exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, tell us: Following the breakthrough by the enemy which breached your defence line, was it the Muslim army or the Serbian army that collected dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims collected theirs and the Serbs collected their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you oversee the gathering of the casualties by Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't able to see them do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the enemy soldiers gathered their dead and took them along as they passed through your territory?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It was when we -- during this activity, we would receive word from our own soldiers of the casualties that we had and wherever we went in the area of Baljkovica where the command post was situated, and there about, we never came across a single Muslim casualty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And as you were searching the terrain for casualties, did you find any Muslim victims in the area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, geographically speaking, how far did the Muslim column stretch that passed through your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean which particular geographical area they traversed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'd like to know where they were able to collect their dead. In other words, when the truce came into force, where was the head and where was the rear of the Muslim column?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were moving from Potocani -- Potocari across Baljkovica where our command post was, across Jeremica hill in the direction of Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we have an interpretation issue. The location that the witness identified is Potocani with an N, not Potocari with an R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Ristic? You were talking about Potocani? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Potocani near Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you aware of any of the developments taking place at the time outside of your area of responsibility and beyond your rear?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew the extent that we were told in the telegram radioed to us by the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer this question: At which geographical point was the rear of the Muslim column at a point when they were allowed passage through the corridor?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my positions, which is the point where the 4th and the 6th Battalions met, after we left Baljkovica and the command, from my vantage point I was able to see Jeremica hill and a part of our command without the rear. In other words I was able to see the house that we used as our headquarters. So I couldn't see the length of the column but I did see them as they were passing by in great numbers across the Jeremica hill. I couldn't see the rest because the view was obstructed by the hill. So I couldn't see the stretch beyond Jeremica hill all the way to Potocani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for us to understand and for Their Honours to understand, can you tell us what the length of the column was as you saw it pass through the area of responsibility of your battalion and how long did it take for them to traverse the area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my vantage point, I was able to assess its length at some 500 metres, so that was its approximate length. And the width was at times up to 20 metres. Later on we were able to observe the track along which they passed where the grass had been trodden upon. Now, how long did it take them to move along, I don't know, perhaps an hour, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But if you could recall the time it took for them to pass through would be -- because that would be important, 500 metres could be travelled in ten minutes but could be travelled in more.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on foot, in a column, so they weren't very fast. It took them maybe around one hour. And maybe I also wasn't present there the whole time because I had to report to the brigade commander. He was in the area of Delici. I was tasked to go across Crni Vrh and pass through the positions of our 7th Battalion to reach the 3rd Company so that after the Muslims had passed from Srebrenica we could then re-establish the line as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in order for us, the participants in these proceedings, to understand the events that you're testifying about, you should tell us who ordered you to stop fighting, to begin a truce, who was it who allowed the Muslims to pass through your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic was with me. He was in command of that operation in Baljkovica. He was ordered to do that, as I heard personally, by the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko [Realtime transcript read in error "Niko"] Pandurevic. He said that the column should be left to pass through and that nobody should open fire until everybody passed. And we obeyed this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question for clarification? You said, Mr. Ristic, on page 38, line 9 and 10, "It took them maybe around one hour." What does that mean? One hour to get from where to where? Could you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Potocari to Nezuk. Because from Potocari to the Jeremica hill, there is one to one and a half kilometre, and then there is another 500 metres across the Jeremica hill, then they had to go down towards a stream, towards Nezuk, and since it was a large column, they couldn't really move very fast. Also, there were some other people who were catching up with the column as they went, so that's why the corridor was closed only the day after, in the afternoon because not everybody was in Potocari. Some people would pass later so we waited for them to pass through as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said you couldn't see the full length of the column. From where to where did you have sight on the column? Which part of this full passage from Potocari to Nezuk you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was watching from our trenches at Parlog and I was looking at the Jeremica hill and our line of defence. Its length was about 500 metres. I have to apologise because this is just my estimation. I think it was around 500 metres. So I observed the column for a while. I was also resting there. So I spent some half an hour to one hour there and all that time I was observing the column passing by. And then I was called and tasked with another task. Had they not called me I would probably stayed there and watched it until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm on my feet only for a couple of minor issues. One was with respect to the references in page 39, I have it as line 6 through 12 to Potocari, again it's the same issue, I think it should read Potocani with an N. And also on page 38, line 23, the reference to Pandurevic should be Vinko definitively and not Niko, N-i-k-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us the exact date and the exact time, if you know, when the corridor was open to allow the Muslim column to pass and also the exact date and the exact time when the corridor was closed? You said that it took one day and one night. So can we have it more precise?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor was opened on the 16th of July 1995, between 13 and 1400 hours. It was closed on the 17th of July in the afternoon. I'm not able to give you more precise time. It was afternoon, it was summer, so maybe it was even 1600 or 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did they all pass through the zone of responsibility of your battalion, your unit?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you receive any favour from the Muslims for the fact that you opened this corridor or was it simply an intermission in combat activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a conversation between Vinko Pandurevic and their commander, Semso Muminovic. They talked through Captain Jolovic's Motorola. And the counter-favour was that they would return all the prisoners from our side that the Muslims in Srebrenica had. That's exactly what happened. They caught one of our mortar men and they returned him. So this Semso was I don't know exactly at what place but I have to say that this person was returned the same day. He called us up, told us that he had one captured soldier and that we should come and take him over. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So was it the only counter-favour, they only released this one person for all those people who went through your zone?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I know. Now, whether there was something else, whether something else was agreed, I don't know. The only thing that I know that the one person who surrendered to our command on the 16th, around 1700 hours, was from one of the detachments from Srebrenica, and then when Major Obrenovic asked him, How many of you are there, he replied in writing because he was unable to speak that there was 5.000 civilians and 2.000 men of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your soldiers -- did your battalion determine how many armed people passed through your zone during this movement of the column?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was hard to determine that because they were hiding, this column was trying not to be observed. The following day, in the zone of Poljane when we had to re-establish the line, I was able to observe and other people saw it too, that around our command, a large number of armed Muslim soldiers passed. Now, I cannot say whether they were from Srebrenica or whether they came from the 2nd Corps, having heard that the passage had been opened, but there were many of them and they also passed without being hindered towards Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order for the participants in these proceedings to understand that the Muslim army passed through your defence zone, and you were not able to count them, are we to understand that they didn't go in single file but in groups?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago that later on we went to check their traces. We even tried to measure what was the width of the footpath that they used in their passage and it was about 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I understood that you said that the footpath was 20 metres wide but what was the width of the corridor, the corridor that your soldiers were not allowed to enter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The width of the corridor was around one kilometre, because you know there is one part from Rijeka Baljkovacka that we hadn't occupied because it's a swamp and it's very close to the river, Rijeka Baljkovacka. So we moved one company or two squads which were there so if you take all this into account, I think that the width would be around one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any damage to any Serbian settlement caused by the movement of the column across this axis?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only Serbian area there is Baljkovica. It had been destroyed earlier in 1992 so the only thing there was the defence line. There wasn't a single Serbian village from Crni Vrh to Nezluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any military conscripts or civilians from the village of Baljkovica who lost their lives during the period that the Muslim armed column was passing through your defence zone?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether there was somebody from Baljkovica. I know some people who were casualties in that area. So during their passage and later, because there were some groups that were a bit late, we lost about 20 people and though some were wounded, I think in total we had about 40 people until the end of it, including military police as well. People from Vukovi Sa Drine and the 7th Battalion which was on our left side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted, if you can explain for me, the difference -- in the context of your testimony, the difference between - hang on - the footpath and the corridor. And I ask this question in the context of what you said at page 42, line 8, which is as follows: "We even tried to measure what was the width of the footpath." And then in line 13, you say, "The width of the corridor was around one kilometre." So what's the difference between the footpath and the corridor in the context of that testimony? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a difference. The corridor is the zone of the 1st Company. The corridor itself had to be wider so that our soldiers would not be close to the people in the column. Otherwise there could be skirmishes and, you know, brawls and other things. That is why we opened the corridor so wide so that those who were passing through it could pass through it without hindrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: All right. So where was the footpath, in the middle of your corridor or on the side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was first on the side, because they were trying to hide behind the hill, and then later on, which axis they took, I wouldn't know. Closer to our line they were relatively near the river. I don't know whether some of them knew the territory or not, but there were very, very few dugouts in that area, only one, so I assume that near Poljane they tried to avoid our people. Then on the other segment, the path was marked because we saw it later and they had their own people who took them over and escorted them to Nezluk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, we are using different terms here, a corridor, a passage, a footpath. So can you tell us could we say that until the truce was in effect we can talk about the breakthrough, and after that we can talk about the corridor within which there were footpaths used by them to actually pass?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had to leave the command. Until that moment we can talk about the breakthrough. We had to leave it because of the attack of the Muslim forces from Srebrenica. So we withdrew involuntarily and that part from the command up to our line, it's about 300 metres, that part was later on opened as the corridor. And they managed to break through all the way to the point 300 metres from our line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe my question was not precise. When the Prosecutor asked you, he used certain terms, he said the Muslim column passed and he even added that it passed with great casualties. Does that point to the conclusion that we are confusing the breakthrough and the open corridor? Up to the truce it was a breakthrough, and after the truce, it was the corridor. Would you be willing to call it a corridor before the truce?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not break through the defence lines, they just destroyed the command and then Commander Pandurevic and Semso Muminovic on the other side agreed that a corridor should be opened up. Now, whether Pandurevic knew or did not know that the command had fallen and why that was done in the way it was, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
