utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, whether you know what the overall losses in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade were and whether they were higher than the losses in the combat and the fighting of your units within a month or an annual period?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned later on that there were some 40 or 42 fatalities, members of the Zvornik Brigade, that those were the losses. Now, whether that was the biggest loss, I wouldn't really know. I don't know what the situation was like in other theatres of war. But I know for sure that our losses were 40 or 42 dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us how many dead did you have within your battalion in the course of 1995, not including those who were killed during the fighting to establish or open up the corridor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have losses. In the four years of fighting in that area, this was the first and the biggest battle that we fought in this area where I was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the other units that were defending Republika Srpska and that were deployed in the same positions where you were deployed? Did they have bigger losses in those four years of fighting than on this one single day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I don't have that information. I don't know what the brigade losses were. I wasn't privy to such information, and I didn't inquire about it, and I don't know what happened in other theatres of war, so I can't really give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I wasn't accurate enough in my question. I'm not asking you about the total brigade losses. I'm asking you about the total losses on this portion of the front line where you were defending yourself against the Muslim army. Were there any bigger losses incurred or suffered by your brigade than on that one single day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't -- there weren't any bigger losses, as far as the Zvornik Brigade is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, as battalion commander, were these the most -- was this the most intense fighting in your area of responsibility? In other words, when they were breaking through and advancing and you were also being attacked from the rear?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the most intense fighting in the period that I was there in the 4th Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ristic, I thank you for your answers. And I have no further questions for you. My cross-examination is complete.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, I would like to tell you too that I have no further questions for this witness and I wish the witness a safe trip home and may God bless you. Your Honour, I would also like to tender D -- 1D556 and 1D557 into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Both documents will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned exhibit numbers D149 and D150 respectively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do I have some redirect examination, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. I mixed the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. It wasn't intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I just want to start off where General Tolimir's just ended briefly, Mr. Ristic. You've indicated that you -- your battalion, the position of your battalion was attacked from the rear and also attacked from the front and you were asked about the objectives of the attack from the front, that is from the units of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH. Were you able to re-establish the position, the original positions, of the defence lines following the opening of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it wasn't the case that they were seized or those positions were actually taken by the ABiH 2nd Corps during the course of the attack?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They withdrew from our trenches on the 17th in the afternoon, most probably around 5.00 p.m., and we reentered our trenches without any opposition, and we had occasion then to get quite close to them because they were waiting to withdraw and we to retake our trenches. We could even talk to them. We exchanged a few words. But there was no exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you also indicated in response to a question by General Tolimir that the concession that you received, that is, the VRS received, in exchange for the opening of the corridor was the return of a prisoner. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who the prisoner was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the mortar crew. His name was Mile Tesic. I'm sure about his last name but I believe his first name is Mile also, so Mile Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not the VRS or the members of your battalion or your brigade at any point from the time that you first became aware that there were prisoners in the school until the time that your commander returned on the 18th, exchanged any prisoner within its custody?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any exchanges of prisoners other than in the area of my -- in my area of responsibility involving Mile Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about the possibility of exchange, that is of the prisoners that were brought to the Orahovac school or in the general area of your battalion. I want to ask you a couple of questions about that, if I may. Would it be the case that you, functioning as the commander of the 4th Battalion, should have been aware of any exchange that was to take place in the area of responsibility of the 4th Battalion, in advance of the exchange itself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief Obrenovic and commander Pandurevic called me on that occasion to ask me whether I knew whether there were any prisoners or any missing men, whether my soldiers had seen that anyone was taken away and that we should report that to their -- to them so that they could tell their commander, Muminovic, so that that person could be returned. I was told on that occasion that Boro Stojic, one of our men who was actually leading a horse carrying food, that he was -- had been wounded and taken over. I conveyed that to the commander and they were told that there was no such man in their captivity. However, a few hours later that man reappeared but whether he had just pretended he was dead or laid low in the meantime or whatever had transpired in the meantime, I don't know, but he did appear. That's all I was asked about and that's what I knew was happening in the area of responsibility of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so we are clear this was after the 14th of July 1995 that you're talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the corridor was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of the prisoners that were brought to the school, the Orahovac school, had they been brought there for exchange, that is something that you as the acting battalion commander, as the deputy battalion commander, should known about or should have been told about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained why they should have told me, but as for any exchanges or bringing in prisoners to Orahovac, I -- they didn't have to inform me of that because that was not within my area of responsibility. The Orahovac school was, according to their plans, in the event of an attack on the Zvornik Brigade, that school was supposed to be the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, and in the event of a major attack or an attack on the command post, that area was reserved for their use and we from the battalion had nothing to do with the school building or that part of Orahovac, other than that Orahovac soldiers were members of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Mr. Ristic. But my question is fundamentally this: Had those prisoners been brought to the Orahovac school for the purposes of being exchanged across your defence lines, isn't this something that should have been told to you in advance of bringing them there or at the very least shortly after their arrival there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had there been any talk of exchanges to take place in our territory, I would have probably been informed and instructed as to how to provide security and how to carry that out. However, I assume that it hadn't been planned to occur in that -- through that area, through that area of responsibility. There was mention of Batkovic or another area, I don't know, but there was no talk about any exchanges of prisoners of war through our territory where I was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Doesn't the fact that you, as the battalion deputy commander, in charge of the battalion during that period of time, doesn't the fact that you weren't told about an exchange tell you something about whether any exchange was actually intended for the prisoners in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was probably no intention to carry out exchanges in my area of responsibility because in the previous years of the war, it had never been done in that area. I don't know why not but it never occurred there. It was usually on a major road on the way to Tuzla or in Bijeljina, but in the area where I was it was difficult -- that would have been difficult because the terrain was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So from a military point of view, it would have been an unsuitable location to conduct an exchange in any event? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned Batkovic how far is Batkovic camp from, let's say, the Orahovac school, the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Bijeljina is about 50 kilometres away from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how far would that be in terms of time, were you to travel from Zvornik to Bijeljina by road?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on how you were travelling, but if you were to go by bus, it would probably take an hour. If you were to travel by car, probably faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And of your -- well, in your knowledge or in your experience, are you aware of exchanges that were conducted from Batkovic , that is of prisoners that were held there, during the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard earlier that there were exchanges in Batkovic, that's what I heard, and I knew that there were exchanges in that area, exchanges of prisoners, and there were smaller groups exchanged also in Memici on the Zvornik-Tuzla communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the exchange of prisoners in Batkovic, first of all do you know whether prisoners were registered when they were held in Batkovic, just generally?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I don't know how that is done. I don't have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the ICRC registering prisoners brought up to Batkovic that were subsequently exchanged, at all, during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later on, maybe even at that time, that the ICRC was involved in this but I wasn't present so I don't know if that's how it actually was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the information that you had on the 14th of July 1995, is there any reason, militarily speaking, why an exchange could not have been conducted from Batkovic or through Batkovic of the prisoners that you -- that you gained knowledge of were being held in your area of responsibility and in the area of responsibility of the brigade generally?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was any other fighting going on at the time in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik or Bijeljina brigades. The only thing going on at the time was in Srebrenica, in the area of the Drina Corps. Now, why that wasn't carried out in that way, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few other questions concerning these prisoners. You were asked by General Tolimir -- I don't have the exact transcript reference but I think everyone will recall it -- a question about whether it was possible that the plans changed in relation to these prisoners essentially from the possibility of their exchange to ultimately what was their execution. You may remember that and I objected to that question. What I want to ask you about is you've indicated in your prior testimony and again today that -- that you are familiar with what Major Obrenovic has said about these prisoners. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think you indicated in your prior testimony, and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, that you actually read the statement of facts that he gave in relation to his plea concerning the events at issue in this case. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me one second. I'd like to show you 65 ter 7023.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I did not use Obrenovic's statement during the cross-examination. So it cannot be used as the basis for re-examination. And the reason I didn't use it is that this witness gave his own direct answers to the questions put by the investigator as to why he did not agree with the statement of facts as Obrenovic set them out in his statement. So I would -- I think that this statement cannot be used for re-examination on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think -- well, let me just say, General Tolimir is fundamentally incorrect about the usage of the document. He put to the witness in no uncertain terms that there was the possibility that these prisoners that had been brought to the area of Zvornik were destined to be exchanged, that there was that possibility, and the fact that they ended up all executed could have been the result of a change in the plan. This document is directly responsive to that. It is directly responsive to this witness's understanding of the events that occurred during that period of time, and directly -- it directly related to that possibility, that is the potential for a plan to have changed or not have changed, which is exactly the issue that was raised on cross-examination. Moreover, the statement that General Tolimir has introduced into evidence concerning this witness's prior statements directly address this particular statement of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber -- Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber has discussed the positions and would like to rule on this. But you want to add something? Please do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The basis for my question to the witness was his statement on page 41 in Serbian and page 31 in English, which is document 1D556, lines on the pages that I just mentioned, 26 through 30. And I even quoted him. That was the basis for what Mr. Nikolic told the witness, Mr. Ristic. That was the foundation for my question, and not any additional statement that the Prosecutor, Mr. Vanderpuye, has mentioned here. And that is why I submitted my complaint. Thank you. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We understood your position, Mr. Tolimir. However, it is a typical situation in re-examination that a certain part of the testimony during cross-examination may be challenged by other documents than used during cross-examination. You were asking the witness about his impression of a possible change of the intention of his superiors in relation to these prisoners. And now, Mr. Vanderpuye is dwelling on that and is using another document which the Chamber doesn't know at the moment but the Chamber is of the view that it should be used to deal with this part of cross-examination Mr. Vanderpuye was indicating. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I had asked for 65 ter 7023 in e-court. All right. First I just want to clarify with you that you have in fact read this statement of fact of Dragan Obrenovic. I can see it here in the transcript of your interview from 18th October, I believe it was 2005. I only have the English reference but it's page 16 and it's D149 now in evidence, page 16 in the English, where you've indicated that you read Obrenovic's statement on the internet. First let me just clarify. This is the statement that you read, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- well, your interview was back in 2005 so clearly you read it before then; is that fair to say? Can you tell us approximately when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly. It may have been in 2004 or early 2005 that I had an opportunity to read the statement on line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can Mr. Vanderpuye say why the statement was made and in what context, now that he's already using it as part of his redirect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think those issues will become very clear to General Tolimir in the context of the face. It says on its face that it was submitted in the context of a plea agreement between Dragan Obrenovic and the Office of the Prosecutor. It's written there on the document itself so I think that's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to do is I want to point out a couple of things about the statement to the witness. You see in the first paragraph Obrenovic states that he became aware of the Muslim prisoners coming up to the Zvornik area on the evening of 13 July 1995. He says he receives a phone call at about 1900 from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, and that Nikolic called from the brigade's forward command post and told him that he had just been telephoned by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. Let me stop right there and ask you, do you know who Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is -- or was back in July of 1995, what his position was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the Popovic from the corps, I heard that he was a security organ of the corps. At a time when I was still within the security department I heard of a Popovic working in the security department of the corps, if that is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. He goes on to say that Drago Nikolic, relayed to him, that is Obrenovic, that Popovic told him that a number of Muslim prisoners were to arrive in Zvornik from Bratunac and that Drago Nikolic was to make preparations for their arrival. He says he understood that a huge number of Muslim prisoners, meaning thousands of Muslim prisoners -- that this was the number of individuals that was supposed to come up there. And he says he received earlier in the day information that thousands had been captured down in the Konjevic Polje area. He goes on to say Drago Nikolic said that he had to be relieved from the forward command post to carry out this task and he told Obrenovic that Popovic was going to send someone to brief him in person and give him additional information. He then says that he asked why the prisoners were not being transported further north to the prisoner of war camp at Batkovici and Nikolic tells him that they were not going to send the prisoners to Batkovici because the Red Cross knew about Batkovici, and said that the orders were that the prisoners were to be brought to Zvornik to be shot. He then goes on to say that he told Drago Nikolic that we, meaning the brigade, would not -- could not accept responsibility for the task that he had just informed him of without informing the command and that Drago Nikolic told him that the command already knew and that the order came from Mladic and everyone including Pandurevic was aware of the order. Having read this, Mr. Ristic, before being asked by General Tolimir about the possibility that these prisoners would have been exchanged on the 14th, doesn't this tell you that the prisoners were in Orahovac to be shot and not to be exchanged, in clear and certain terms?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you my opinion of it all. If they were supposed to be shot, then they could have been shot in Konjevic Polje and Kamenica areas where there were no civilians, there was no army, or defence line to man. Why would someone bring these people into an inhabited area close to the front line within the area of responsibility or close to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps when they had intercepted conversations indicating that columns would be moving along Snagovo, Crni Vrh, Krizevacke Njive, Baljevica [phoen] to Nezuk? It seemed an odd decision to make, to bring these people over with an intention to shoot them. I believe that the intention was for these people to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you're telling this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That somebody changed the plan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes that's what the witness added.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you're telling this Trial Chamber that with an army facing your front and thousands of people, including armed individuals coming from behind you, in a mountainous area, in a potentially militarily vulnerable area in the area of Zvornik would have been a better place to conduct an exchange? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what your understanding of what I said was but I didn't talk about the exchange in reference to this area. What I said was that my belief was that they were to spend a short while in the school because they -- the intention was to have them subsequently exchanged. But what I said was that it would have been impracticable to carry out exchanges of so many people in this mountainous area, with poor communications, and it would have been a dangerous thing to attempt to do something like that there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies. I didn't want to interrupt earlier on. I don't want to leave an impression that I don't want to analyse these facts. However, I don't think it is appropriate to have this person and his brothers in arms accused of something in reference to a statement that was part of a plea agreement. I don't think the witness should be further examined on this point. He gave his opinion and that's an end to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has ruled on that. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you've just said about the prisoners being held at the school to be later exchanged was something that Drago Nikolic told you about when you spoke to him about these prisoners, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in fact, I think you said in your 18th October statement that you spoke to Drago Nikolic some ten to 20 days after the events in Orahovac. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Did you know, first, that prisoners were brought to the Orahovac school beginning on the evening of the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know that an execution of thousands -- of at least a thousand individuals, Muslims, had occurred at the Kravica warehouse on the evening/afternoon, late afternoon, I would say, of 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Momir Nikolic stated that he had information from Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, security chief of the Drina Corps, that there was an intention to separate out men, military-aged men, and for them to be executed; on the 12th of July he had that information? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I was positioned in an area far away from all these events, and as I said, my command and my battalion were exclusively occupied with the defence effort. Nobody conveyed the information to me. I didn't seek information. And I didn't know what was happening in relation to Srebrenica after its fall. Everything that I knew came from the telegram we received, which said that the attack on Srebrenica commenced, that it fell on the 12th of July, and my battalion and I had no further information because we were up there at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is being asked about the statements given by individuals who entered into agreements with the OTP rather than about his personal knowledge of the events of the 13th and the 14th in the areas where he and his unit were deployed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness was asked about one statement given by one individual, indeed that's true. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you know, Witness -- did you know that on the 13th of July, when those prisoners began moving up into your area, the Orahovac school, that elements of the UN were still down in the area of Srebrenica, Potocari, Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, and other international organisations as well? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time, but later on, through various stories, I heard of the Dutch Battalion, I was able to read about some things, but at that time, on the 13th, 14th, and the 15th, I didn't have information about the goings on in Srebrenica. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, now I think you are in danger to leave the area of topics addressed during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In danger, perhaps, but I don't think I'm quite there yet. I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm always very careful in formulating this but I haven't heard anything about these facts on international troops present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should remove his headphones, if I may, I can explain to the Trial Chamber exactly the nature and the relevance of this area of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have no doubt that all this is relevant for the case but the problem is we are now in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to redirect, I can explain that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, could you please take your ear-phones off for a moment? Mr. Vanderpuye wants to address something for the Chamber. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the reason why this area of examination is directly germane to the cross-examination is precisely because what General Tolimir has suggested through the cross-examination is that the prisoners were brought first to the school and during some period of time while they were at the school, some plan developed to execute them which was not in place at the time that they were brought there. I've asked the witness a number of questions about that, you're correct, and he's answered those questions. He's suggested in answering to one of those questions that there was the possibility that these prisoners could have been shot in the area of Konjevic Polje which is precisely the area that I'm now discussing, the area south of Zvornik, where they were originally, Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, and so on, that there was the possibility that if an execution was intended it could be carried out there. He's now said that he has information that during that same period of time, that area, in that area, I should say, there were international organisations, the UN was still there, there was an area that was under observation of the international community which is what I'm establishing at this point. Which does not support the idea that if an execution were to have been intended, it could have been carried out in the area that the witness has suggested it might otherwise have been. That's the nature of the issue. And that I think responds directly to General Tolimir's general question whether or not there was a change of plan between the time that the prisoners were sent to the area of Zvornik and the time that they were ultimately executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we considered your position, including your explanation why you put this question to the witness. I think the way you have put the -- this question is not appropriate during re-examination. If you rephrase your question and refer exactly to what the witness has answered earlier during the re-examination, especially to this sentence, "If they were supposed to be shot then they could have been slot in Konjevic Polje and Kamenica areas where there are no civilians." If you relate your question to this area, then there is a link to be seen by everybody, by the parties and even the witness. The way you put the question was very surprising and I think you should rephrase it to get a proper answer in the course of your re-examination. Now I would like to ask the witness to take the ear-phones again. Mr. Vanderpuye, I was referring to the answer of the witness, page 58, lines 12 through 21, especially the first three or four lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And I do appreciate it. I didn't have the specific transcript reference in front of me when I put the question but I think I can probably frame it a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, when I asked you about the statement of facts of Dragan Obrenovic, and in particular I asked you whether what you could read from the first four paragraphs of the document makes it clear that the prisoners that were brought to Orahovac were brought there to be shot, you responded that -- you said: "I can give you my opinion of it all. If they were supposed to be shot they could have been shot in Konjevic Polje and Kamenica areas where there were no civilians. There was no army or defence lines to man." And what I'm asking you about now is, having said that, did you know that in the areas where you said that they could have been shot, that there were still elements of the UN, or other international organisations, at that time? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know where these -- any of these parties were located. I told you that this was my opinion but now I do see that there is a problem there. But nevertheless, I still claim that they were not supposed to be taken to the area of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you 65 ter 2579. Actually, let me change that. Let me show you a different document instead. It's P00014 and what I want to show you is page 124 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English. Before I get to the point of my -- of this document, let me just ask you a couple of questions. You were asked on redirect in response to the direct examination, about your knowledge of the executions that took place in Orahovac in particular, I asked you some questions about the area in which an exhumation was conducted that you became aware of subsequently. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware that the executions in Orahovac were followed by the burial, the creation of a mass grave and the burial of the individuals that were executed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the prisoners that were killed in Orahovac were buried in a mass grave? That a grave was dug out and that they were buried in it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that I saw it when it was dug up by members of SFOR or IFOR, I don't know who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm showing you here is an entry in the duty officer logbook of the Zvornik Brigade. You were asked some questions about the purpose of the duty officer by General Tolimir, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular, you indicated that the duty officer basically fielded issues because the commander couldn't respond to every issue that came to the brigade command. And that's a paraphrase but is that roughly right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an entry in the duty officer's logbook for the Zvornik Brigade from 13 July, it's the Prosecution's position that it is a 13 July entry, for -- for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, we will obviously introduce evidence to substantiate that. And in this particular entry, I'll refer you to I think it's at the bottom of the page, it indicates here, "Vukotic needs to call Aco and Aco" - you can see there is an arrow, it says, it looks like "Dzafin Kamen needs to be dispatched to the 4th Battalion." Do you see that entry? It's just above the last paragraph of the page and the sentence begins with "Vukotic." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Below that you see an entry that states, "Stevo Kostic to get in contact with Aco" and then it says, "President of the municipality, Mitrovic, called and asked that the flat bed trailer" - and then you can see it says, "Beara" - Colonel Beara, crossed out - "be sent to Bratunac to bring a bulldozer, 1.000, Colonel Beara passed on the message." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The use of a bulldozer during that period of time, it is the position of the Prosecution, was for the purpose of carrying out burials. Would this entry suggest to you that there was any plan to exchange the prisoners that were brought to the school in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't related to the plan. As far as this individual Aco is concerned, I presume that he was a man from the military police who came to help us by bringing along a number of his military policemen to provide security for our mortars, because the individuals who had arrived there earlier on had to leave for Snagovo on the 13th or the 14th. That was the 3rd infantry platoon that was sent by Major Obrenovic, was dispatched there because Krizevacke Njive is close to the feature Grujica hill where our mortars were positioned. So there man Aco from the military police if that's where he came from, came to help us out and between the 14th and the 15th, or the 15th and the 16th, he was withdrawn all the way to our command post and together we left Baljkovica on the 16th. He was even wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Beara is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the end of the interpretation and now Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My objection is as follows: This witness is now not being asked about his personal observations. The questions are being asked of him about some other people's writing in a book that he did not have, a book that he did not write, the book that does not talk about his unit. Thank you. And I would really like for this to stop in order to somehow impute some responsibility to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you were saying you are going to substantiate the discussion about the duty -- of the duty officer, and the relation to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Substantiate, yes, the authenticity and the reliability of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please, I have not finished. Now, you are going into details of the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure if this is, during re-examination, the right course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The reason why I'm going into the entries, Your Honour, is to the extent that there is a suggestion that there was no plan in place to execute the prisoners that were brought to the Zvornik area, given the witness's experience, both as a battalion commander and as an assistant -- former assistant commander for security and intelligence, and given the witness's understanding of what the role of a duty operations officer is within the brigade, whether or not this particular entry, and I'll get to it, relating to Colonel Beara, chief of security of the Main Staff of the VRS as concerns the use of bulldozers and flat bed trucks on 13 July 1995, in advance of the execution of the prisoners on 14 July 1995, bears upon the likelihood that these prisoners were to be exchanged on the 14th of July as suggested during the course of the cross-examination. And I think he's in a position to say whether or not, in his mind, it bears on that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was hoping that we can finish the examination of this witness before the second break. I think this is not possible. We must have the second break now, and Mr. Vanderpuye, can you give us an estimation of the remaining time you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have one other document besides this to show him and about four or five questions related to that. I think it shouldn't take more than 15 minutes to do. I'm usually a little bit overly optimistic but I think that's about fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is our impression from the examination-in-chief already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now and we will resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before the break, you indicated you want to respond to the Prosecution. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that now there is no need for that because Mr. Vanderpuye indicated that he was about to move on to another subject. What I wanted to say was that the questions posed so far were the questions for examination-in-chief and not for cross-examination. I simply wanted to ask him to move on to cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think you are in re-examination and Mr. Tolimir, in fact, was referring to re-examination. You should continue but the Chamber is -- would appreciate if you could put your questions in a way that we always see the nexus to the questions put by Mr. Tolimir during cross-examination, as it was the case earlier when we -- when you were dealing with UN troops and DutchBat battalion, it is necessary for the Chamber, at least, but also for Mr. Tolimir, to see there is a nexus to part of the cross-examination. If you go ahead with the last 15 minutes, please bear that in mind, especially if you use new documents not used during examination-in-chief and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I think we had a -- yes, we still do have the duty officer notebook on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, I'd asked you in my last question to you regarding this notebook was: Do you know who Colonel Beara is or at least was at the time in July 1995, what his position is?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know the members of the Main Staff. I did not know their functions. But during the war, I heard of a Colonel Beara in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear what his position was in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about him, I did not meet him, I did not see him during the war, so I wasn't even interested in his function. I really don't know what were the functions of people in the Main Staff. That was far away from me. I didn't even know about the corps, let alone the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I want to show you one other document, it's 65 ter 2579. And while we are getting that up, I just want to ask you about this entry in the duty officer logbook. You mentioned someone named Aco as a military policeman. Do you remember talking about that just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the individual named Stevo Kostic also in that entry in the logbook, do you know who he is or what he -- what his position was back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the military police. I think he was a clerk in the military police. I don't know whether that was the exact name of his function, but he handled papers and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know whether either Aco or Stevo Kostic were either directly or indirectly, shall we say, involved with the prisoners or with the events that occurred in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at the document we have now on the screen in front of us. This is a document entitled, "Instructions concerning the work of," and the translation reads, "deputy battalion commander for intelligence and security." You can tell me if it might be a more accurate translation that it reads "assistant commander for intelligence and security"?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant battalion commander for intelligence and security work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That would be consistent with the position that you occupied between 1993, March, and 1995, March; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This particular document is attributable to Drago Coric do you know who Drago Coric is?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was his position when you knew him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was also for a while an assistant commander. I don't know in which battalion but he was also assistant battalion commander for security. I don't know which battalion. I think that we attended some meetings in the brigade together and that that's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say in a battalion, you mean a battalion within the Zvornik Brigade or some other brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions just about this document, since General Tolimir put to you some questions concerning your duties and functions as was contained in the brigade rules for security, I think, is what he showed you. In particular, let me refer you to the functions it says here as assistant -- as -- your intelligence functions. You should see that under item number 1. If we go down the page a little bit, you will see in an underlined section, it reads, that "He," meaning the assistant commander for security and intelligence, "Shall carry out the necessary interrogation of war prisoners and refugees and arrange for their evacuation to a determined place." Do you see that there, among several other functions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your understanding of your functions or your responsibilities while you were assistant commander for security and intelligence in the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does. However, when I was at this function, I had no chance to interrogate anybody because there were no captured prisoners while I was an assistant commander for intelligence and security work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Immediately above that, you can see that it reads that: "The assistant commander for security and intelligence shall organise general use of intelligence data in the battalion and immediately inform the battalion commander about all important data on the enemy. He shall inform his superior and neighbouring intelligence and security organs." Is that also consistent with your understanding of your responsibilities while you were serving within the security organ of -- at the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to item number 2, which is at the bottom of the page in the English and I think at the top of the next page in the B/C/S. And here, under this section, it talks about the functions in the security capacity, and lists a number of tasks. Among them I'd like to refer you to about the middle of the page and it reads as follows: "He," meaning the assistant commander for security and intelligence, "Shall undertake measures to detect and arrest perpetrators of criminal acts in the areas of the responsibility of security organs of the armed forces, as well as measures to uncover and secure evidence of criminal acts or objects which may serve as evidence. And he shall gather all information which may be useful for successfully conducting criminal proceedings." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that consistent with the understanding -- with your understanding of your functions during the period of time that you were assistant commander for security and intelligence in the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, then, that a security officer would or should be aware of information concerning the presence of prisoners of war or prisoners and refugees and has a responsibility with respect to the detection of crimes concerning those prisoners within the confines, in your case, of the battalion, the area of responsibility of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would hold if our command was in Orahovac and if all this was in our zone of responsibility or in Baljkovica where we were situated. However, since we were ten or more kilometres away from Zvornik, across mountains, I assumed that somebody thought that we did not know -- we did not need to know all this because all this was probably organised at the level of the brigade and not the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that your understanding of the responsibilities of a security and intelligence officer within the security and intelligence administrations or sectors would call for any such officer, at the relevant unit level, brigade, battalion, corps, Main Staff, to undertake the responsibilities that are set out in this document, that is, involvement with prisoners, at least at the level of interrogation, or evacuation, and that is, in terms of undertaking measures to detect and arrest perpetrators of criminal acts in the area of the relevant responsibility or the relevant area of responsibility? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already described my role, what I was doing in my battalion, that I described the role of the battalion commander and the relationship between our battalion and the brigade. Maybe I should inform the Chamber as well as General that in practice of both battalion and the Zvornik Brigade, we did not have professionally educated officers in the relevant fields of expertise. I, for instance, did not have these instructions, nobody ever gave it to me. That's why I consider that we could not observe such rules because our battalion, that wasn't an army with barracks, with officers with morning lineup, with everything that is prescribed by military rules. Those were just people from nearby villages, people who had to go back home to tend their flocks and their fields and in most cases they would arrive to the defence lines with their own equipment and their own food. And then they would get their tasks from the battalion commander or the company commander. This is how we managed to do things during this war period. We simply relied on our own knowledge. We really didn't work according to some rules and regulations prescribed by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You've indicated that Drago Coric was a member of the Zvornik Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in particular, that he was an assistant commander for security and intelligence at the battalion level, right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure if you can see it very clearly -- if we go to the first page in the B/C/S of this document, but you can see his name at the top of this particular document, written in Cyrillic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so this is information that was within, let's say, the knowledge of the security organ at the battalion level in the Zvornik Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer this question I would like to ask the witness to read the name of this person very slowly into the record because I think it's wrongly stated in the record. What is the name of this man, Drago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drago Cvoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since this document doesn't have the official number, there is no author indicated on it, and no signature, I think that it is improper to claim that this witness should have acted in accordance with the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye is putting the instructions posed which the witness had during the relevant time and the witness answered about his knowledge about the content of the description of his duties but again I have the problem that the name of this man is not recorded again. Please repeat the name very slowly again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] C with a diacritical sign V-O-R-I-C with another diacritical sign. D-R-A-G-O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure it is taped and we can reconstruct it later. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if -- I did not get an answer to my last question and my last question was that this information was within the knowledge of the security organ at the battalion level. Is that fair to say, given the document you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is some sort of instruction for his work that he received and I did not. I don't know whether he took this instruction out of some book that the JNA members used to carry around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness answered. What I wanted to say is how can something like that pertain to this witness? How can you say that he should have known about it when he already stated that he never saw this document before, that he never had this document before and that this Cvoric had no sort of command relationship with him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't hear any question with this content you are quoting. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on but bear in mind now you have reached 24 minutes of your 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just bear with me for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My last question, if we could go to the second page of the B/C/S, please and also the second page of the English? In relation to the part of this document which I read into the record previously where it says: "The assistant commander for security intelligence shall undertake measures to detect and arrest perpetrators of criminal acts in the areas under the responsibility of the security organs of the armed forces, as well as measures to uncover and secure evidence of criminal acts or objects." As concerns the role of an assistant commander of security and intelligence at the battalion level, wouldn't this or does this entail the use of the military police units available either at the brigade level in your case or at any other unit level?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police belong to the brigade. They had their instructions about how to perform their work. I already explained how we worked with the military police. Now, what exactly they were doing directly with the military police in the brigade, I don't know. I was never in the brigade. I spent all my time in the 4th Infantry Battalion, from the very beginning until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my redirect examination. I would like to offer into evidence this document, 65 ter 2579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit number P1760. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes the examination. The Chamber would like to thank you also on behalf of the parties that you were able to come here to The Hague again and to provide us with your knowledge and expertise. Thank you very much. And now you are free to return to your normal activities. Have a safe journey back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, officially welcome Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have only ten minutes left. I think it's not a good idea to start with the next witness because we have to discuss the progress with the witnesses of this week. We see that there are still scheduled three witnesses, two from the region and the witness Blaszczyk. We have only one day of hearings left. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all I was going to suggest what you just suggested. And the two people from the region, well, the next one who is immediately on my mind, who will be handled by Mr. Elderkin is a survivor witness and will be very short from our perspective. And the next person is a more controversial witness in many respects. You remember that's the witness related to the recent motion. And Mr. Blaszczyk was frankly, I don't want to call him a gap filler but he's always available, he's back from knee surgery and ready to go, so we don't need to worry about him. And I just had a couple of -- well, I could say housekeeping matters just for a minute or to address you with before we go but we may not be able to finish that final witness, given I think there seems -- there may be interest in that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first witness tomorrow will be PW-016 in my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I've heard that there are matters to discuss about protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It shouldn't be a problem. We just need to have what he had in Krstic, which was pseudonym and face distortion but apparently we didn't get all that in. We missed -- I think we missed face distortion. We got pseudonym but we missed the face distortion in Krstic so he's a -- it's important that he get what the laws allow him. We've confirmed that that is what he needs and we agree with that and I'm sorry we didn't remind everyone of what was happening in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, this is always unfortunate, this way of receiving notice at the last minute. What is the position of the Defence to the protective measures requested by the Prosecution? I see no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know what Mr. McCloskey is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we can just switch to closed session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The recent testimony regarding the duty officer notebook and the potential for 13 July entry and it reminded me that we owe you the updated versions of the duty officer notebook, teacher's edition, which is in evidence as P1459. You may recall you handed it back to us so that we could correct a few pages that were wrong. So I have the three for the Trial Chamber and the Court officer which, I don't know the difference between court officer and legal officer, I'm sorry, they are both the same in my view. But we can -- we just want to get that to you before the break and I also, lastly, would like to say something that I think the general will agree with me that may help the Court. He has made a statement in one of his questions that the rules that he put on the screen regarding the former JNA rules for the brigade that they were in place at the time of the VRS, it's the Prosecution position we largely agree with that so you know that we don't believe this will be a hard fought issue. I think in most cases we are going to agree that the official rules such as the one the general used for the brigade, for the corps, were generally used by the VRS because they didn't have many of their own rules. And so in that regard, I want to narrow that issue for you so that that shouldn't be something you see us hotly contesting, with perhaps the exception of every once in a while like you saw in the battalion report sometimes they develop their rules, the VRS develops their rules, based on those other rules. So just to narrow those issues for you. I think we will be in agreement. I know our expert has basically said what General Tolimir stated in his question. So I just wanted to help narrow those issues because I know there is a lot of issues out there. The date of the -- when the murder operation was initiated, being one of them, of course, and that's why we spent so much time there, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are there any other matters? If not, my last comment would be I would, and the Chamber would be very happy if the time frame indicated by both parties should be obeyed by and in order to keep this trial as expeditious as possible and we observed several times that, in particular, as I said earlier, the Prosecution had exceeded this time, also with the last witness. Thank you very much. We adjourn and we resume tomorrow morning in this courtroom at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of February 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
